title: Trump Orders US-South Korea Drills Scaled Back as Seoul Refuses Iran War Role; Raytheon Lands $22.9B Tomahawk Deal
subhead: Washington's decision to cut the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises over Seoul's refusal to join the Iran war marks a major shift in the US-ROK alliance posture, while the Pentagon locks in a seven-year Tomahawk production surge and Japan's arms market opens to Europe's Helsing.

sections.heading: US-South Korea Alliance Posture Shifts as Trump Cuts Joint Drills
sections.body:
President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to 'substantially reduce' the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea, which began Monday as scheduled, citing Seoul's refusal to take part in the US war against Iran and his 'very good relationship' with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, Reuters reports. The order, issued in a Truth Social post on Sunday, came hours before the drills were due to start and left unclear which portions would be scaled back.

The move drew immediate bipartisan criticism in Washington. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), a retired Navy captain, called the decision 'shortsighted and a mistake,' while former assistant secretary of state Danny Russel said Trump was 'punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary,' according to India Today. Former diplomat Dan Fried warned the cut 'undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves NATO and emboldens the Chinese.'
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first time in over 70 years a US president has unilaterally curtailed the core US-ROK deterrence exercise, and it signals that alliance commitments are now conditional on participation in Washington's conflicts. It also hands North Korea a diplomatic win and raises questions about extended deterrence credibility across Asia.

sections.heading: Raytheon Locks In $22.9B Tomahawk Deal to Lift Output Past 1,000 a Year
sections.body:
The US military awarded Raytheon, an RTX unit, a $22.9 billion seven-year contract to expand Tomahawk cruise missile production, completing a preliminary framework agreement reached in February, Reuters and The Independent report. Raytheon said the deal will raise annual output to more than 1,000 missiles, up from its present rate of about 60 per year. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said the contract ensures 'our warfighters continue to have the lethal firepower they need,' per The Independent.

The award follows earlier contracts this month to accelerate production of Patriot and THAAD interceptor parts, part of the Trump administration's push to use multi-year agreements to induce contractors to invest in expanded capacity after the Iran war drained precision-guided munitions stockpiles.
sections.whyItMatters: The 16-fold production increase reflects how badly the Iran conflict depleted US cruise missile inventories, and the multi-year contracting model signals a structural shift toward long-horizon industrial base commitments rather than annual stopgap buys.

sections.heading: Japan's Arms Market Opens: Helsing Enlists Rakuten to Sell Strike Drones to GSDF
sections.body:
German defense-AI firm Helsing has enlisted Japanese e-commerce and finance giant Rakuten to broker the sale of its unmanned systems to Japan's Ground Self-Defence Forces, Reuters and The Next Web report. At the center is the HX-2, a compact AI-guided strike drone that Japan's military is field-trialing until the end of September. Rakuten is positioning itself as a broker that can walk foreign defense startups through Japan's notoriously opaque procurement system, having previously helped Ukrainian drone-software firm Swarmer show its tech to Japanese units.

The timing reflects Japan's biggest military build-up in decades and its easing of long-standing arms-export and procurement rules earlier this year, which has thrown open a market foreign weapons-makers could barely touch before. Tokyo has committed to lifting defense spending toward postwar-era highs.
sections.whyItMatters: A consumer-tech conglomerate acting as a weapons broker is a measure of how far the defense boom has spread beyond traditional primes, and it signals Japan's reformed procurement system is now actively courting foreign autonomous-weapons suppliers as it races to close a drone gap.

sections.heading: India Leases Two More MQ-9B SeaGuardians to Bridge Surveillance Gap
sections.body: India's Ministry of Defence signed a $203 million (Rs 1,943 crore) contract with General Atomics to lease two MQ-9B SeaGuardian High-Altitude Long-Endurance drones for 30 months for the Indian Navy, WION and the Times of India report. The ministry said the systems will provide persistent ISR coverage over the Indian Ocean Region, strengthening India's ability to monitor and respond to developments across the maritime domain. The lease bridges a gap before India receives its own fleet of 31 MQ-9B drones under a separate $3 billion tri-service procurement deal.
sections.whyItMatters: The lease underscores India's urgency in closing a maritime surveillance gap in the Indian Ocean as it waits for its purchased fleet, and reflects the broader pattern of India using US platforms to accelerate capability while building toward indigenous production.

sections.heading: L3Harris Ousts CEO Kubasik Over Conduct Breach, Names Insider Mehta
sections.body:
L3Harris Technologies said Chairman and CEO Christopher Kubasik left the company after a board investigation found he engaged in conduct inconsistent with the defense contractor's code of conduct, sending shares down 3.3%, Reuters reports. The company named executive Sam Mehta as CEO effective immediately; Mehta had led the Space & Mission Systems and Communications & Spectrum Dominance segments, which together account for about 80% of revenue. Kubasik will not receive severance, benefits or equity awards under a separation agreement.

The exit is unrelated to financial reporting, internal controls or operational performance, L3Harris said. Kubasik, who steered the 2019 L3-Harris merger and acquired Aerojet Rocketdyne for $4.7 billion in 2023, was previously fired as Lockheed Martin's COO over an improper relationship with a subordinate. The company's planned spin-off of its missile solutions unit was postponed last month to at least mid-2027.
sections.whyItMatters: The abrupt leadership change at a top-tier US defense contractor comes amid a period of heavy Pentagon demand and a delayed missile-unit spin-off, adding governance uncertainty to a company central to US munitions and space programs.

sections.heading: Trump Welcomes Mecca Pact as Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan Alliance Takes Shape
sections.body:
President Trump welcomed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed August 7 by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, calling it 'a big, bold and important first step' toward the three countries defending themselves 'in a more meaningful way,' Outlook India reports. The pact, negotiated for about a year against the backdrop of the US-Iran war, establishes that an armed attack against any of the three is treated as an attack against all. It combines Pakistan's military personnel, Turkey's NATO-strength forces and Saudi Arabia's financial and strategic influence in the Gulf.

Indian analysts are assessing the pact's national security implications, and some commentary notes it has exposed fault lines between the UAE and Saudi Arabia along the India-Israel axis.
sections.whyItMatters: The pact, dubbed an 'Islamic NATO' by some observers, represents a significant non-Western collective-security arrangement in the Middle East and South Asia, and its reception in Washington signals US tolerance — even encouragement — of regional powers building their own defense structures.

bottomLine: The dominant development today is Washington's decision to scale back the US-South Korea exercises over Seoul's refusal to join the Iran war — a break with seven decades of alliance practice that signals US security commitments are now conditional on participation in its conflicts. Beneath that, the defense industrial base is moving in two directions at once: the Pentagon is locking in massive multi-year production deals like the $22.9 billion Tomahawk contract to rebuild depleted stocks, while Japan's newly opened arms market and the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan Mecca pact show procurement and alliance structures diversifying beyond the traditional US-led framework. The net picture is a US alliance system being renegotiated deal-by-deal even as Washington pours record sums into its own munitions base.
sources: Reuters, The Independent, India Today, The Next Web, WION, Times of India, Outlook India, AOL/Reuters, Politico, MSN, France24
